target.title: fix(doctor): preserve install policy config
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running `openclaw doctor` to repair a missing configured plugin could have the install-policy decision evaluated against an older process-level configuration snapshot instead of the exact candidate configuration Doctor was repairing.

This matters when Doctor mutates or recovers configuration in-process: plugin discovery and repair use the current candidate, while ClawHub/npm installation previously had to fall back to ambient runtime config for `security.installPolicy`.

## Why This Change Was Made

Doctor now passes its current candidate config through the private missing-plugin repair helper to ClawHub, npm install, and the npm install-to-update retry. This keeps all three policy decisions aligned with the configuration snapshot that selected the repair candidate; it does not change install-policy rules or broaden supported install sources.

## User Impact

Doctor repairs now consistently honor the install policy from the configuration being repaired, including in-process recovery and mutation paths, instead of potentially consulting stale ambient config.

## Evidence

Failing-first regression proof before the source change:

```text
expected undefined to deeply equal { security: { installPolicy: { enabled: true } }, ... }
Tests 2 failed | 81 skipped
```

Real Doctor behavior proof was captured on equivalent patch head `14dfabb504f361c3ddea799c49988abbdd88d27a`, then based on `5aea34ad8c210ddba5a678d64c559da8414baea7`:

- Ran in an isolated temporary `HOME`, `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`, and `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH`
- Used the production CLI config guard to pin an ambient policy that returns `allow`
- Replaced only the on-disk candidate with a policy that returns `block`
- Invoked the production Doctor command entrypoint with `--fix --yes --non-interactive`
- Used a real missing-plugin npm declaration and a published npm spec; the candidate policy blocked the preflight before install side effects

Redacted terminal evidence:

```text
PROOF ambient snapshot command: <temp>/ambient-allow.cjs
PROOF candidate file command: <temp>/candidate-block.cjs
PROOF invoking real doctor command entrypoint with --fix --yes --non-interactive

Failed to install missing configured plugin "guardrail-bridge" from
@openclaw/discord@2026.6.11: blocked by install policy: candidate
policy blocks proof install

PROOF policy invocation log:
CANDIDATE_BLOCK {"targetName":"guardrail-bridge","targetType":"plugin",
"request":{"kind":"plugin-npm","mode":"install",
"requestedSpecifier":"@openclaw/discord@2026.6.11"}}
```

The only conflict was the upstream config type-module rename in the test import; the current `types.js` path and all upstream Codex Supervisor coverage were preserved.

target.title: fix(config): reject unsupported MCP disabled config
target.body:
Closes #103954

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators configured an MCP server with `disabled: true` and OpenClaw silently started the server because only `enabled: false` controls MCP activation.

## Why This Change Was Made

The change migrates the unsupported inverse flag to the canonical enablement setting through `openclaw doctor --fix`, while configuration validation now reports the incorrect key with an actionable replacement. Runtime behavior continues to read only the canonical setting.

## User Impact

Operators receive a clear configuration error instead of unexpectedly spawning an MCP server. Existing boolean `disabled` entries can be repaired automatically with `openclaw doctor --fix`.

## Evidence

### Real isolated CLI proof

Executed from PR head `f53982039f67` with Node `v24.14.0`, using isolated `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH` and `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` values and no real credentials. The configured stdio command was `/usr/bin/touch $MARKER`, so any process start would leave an observable marker.

Before repair, `openclaw config validate --json` exited 1 and reported:

```json
{
  "valid": false,
  "issues": [
    {
      "path": "mcp.servers.proof-disabled.disabled",
      "message": "unsupported key \"disabled\"; use \"enabled: false\" instead, then run \"openclaw doctor --fix\" to migrate existing config"
    }
  ]
}
```

`openclaw doctor --fix --non-interactive` exited 0 and printed:

```text
Legacy config keys detected
- mcp.servers uses the unsupported "disabled" key; use "enabled: false" instead.

Doctor changes
Moved mcp.servers.proof-disabled.disabled true → enabled false.

Updated config: $CONFIG
Doctor complete.
```

The rewritten entry contained the canonical field and no `disabled` key:

```json
{
  "enabled": false,
  "command": "/usr/bin/touch",
  "args": ["$MARKER"],
  "transport": "stdio"
}
```

After repair, `openclaw config validate --json` exited 0 with `{"valid":true,"warnings":[]}`.

For the post-repair process-start check, the marker was removed and the actual MCP runtime probe was run:

```console
$ openclaw mcp probe --json
{
  "servers": {},
  "tools": [],
  "diagnostics": []
}
$ test -e "$MARKER" && echo present || echo absent
absent
```

A named probe also rejected the server before launch: `MCP server "proof-disabled" is disabled ... Run openclaw mcp configure proof-disabled --enable before probing it.`

### Contract and automated validation

- OpenClaw filters `mcp.servers` entries with `enabled: false` before session MCP runtime materialization (`src/agents/bundle-mcp-config.ts`).
- Direct upstream Codex source inspection at [`5c19155cbd93`](https://github.com/openai/codex/commit/5c19155cbd93bfa099016e7487259f61669823ff) confirmed that `enabled` defaults to true, `false` means skip initialization, and the connection manager filters disabled servers before spawning them (`codex-rs/config/src/mcp_types.rs`, `codex-rs/codex-mcp/src/connection_manager.rs`).
- Focused config and doctor tests passed: 237 assertions across the relevant test shards.
- Core TypeScript check passed with `pnpm tsgo:core`.
- Regression coverage verifies both inverse-value migration and preservation of an explicitly configured `enabled` value.

## AI-assisted contribution

Implemented with Codex; targeted tests, core typechecking, direct upstream contract inspection, and isolated real CLI proof were completed before submission.

target.title: fix(agent-runner): use CJK-aware estimateStringChars for tool-result truncation cap
target.body:
Fixes #103847

## What Problem This Solves
The live tool-result truncation cap in `tool-result-truncation.ts` uses raw `text.length` for both the threshold check and proportional budget allocation. CJK text averages ~1 token/character while the codebase uses ~4 chars/token, so CJK-heavy tool results can overshoot their intended token budget by up to 4x without triggering truncation. This means CJK-heavy tool outputs (e.g. from tools returning Japanese/Chinese/Korean text) silently exceed the model's context budget, leading to context overflow and degraded agent behavior.

## Changes
- Import `estimateStringChars()` from `src/utils/cjk-chars.ts`
- `getToolResultTextLength`: use estimated chars for threshold check so CJK text is correctly flagged as oversized
- `truncateToolResultMessage`: use estimated chars for proportional block budget so Latin and CJK blocks receive fair shares
- `truncateToolResultText`: use estimated chars for early-return and cut-point calculation with density-ratio scaling
- Pure ASCII/Latin text is unaffected (estimatedLength === text.length)

## Evidence
- All 122 existing tests in `tool-result-truncation.test.ts` pass
- `oxlint` passes clean on the modified file
- For CJK text: `estimateStringChars("你好世界")` returns ~16 (4 chars × 4x density) vs `text.length` of 4, correctly triggering truncation at the intended token budget
- For ASCII text: `estimateStringChars("hello")` returns 5, identical to `text.length`, so no behavior change for Latin content
- The density-ratio scaling in `densityAdjustedCut` ensures CJK blocks get proportionally smaller raw-char budgets, preventing context overflow while preserving head/tail content

target.title: fix(config): use Object.hasOwn for own-key checks in write-prepare helpers
target.body:
<details>
<summary>Additional instructions</summary>

**MUST:** Keep **Allow edits from maintainers** enabled for this PR so maintainers
can help update the branch when needed.

</details>

## What Problem This Solves

`createMergePatch`, `collectChangedPaths`, and `projectSourceOntoRuntimeShape` in
`src/config/io.write-prepare.ts` used the `in` operator for key membership. `in`
walks the prototype chain, so a key that is **own on one peer and only inherited
on the other** is misclassified during config write preparation.

Concrete failure (one-sided collision):

1. **`createMergePatch`:** own key on `base` + inherited-only key on `target` →
   old code emits the inherited value in the patch; correct own-key semantics
   emit `null` (delete).
2. **`collectChangedPaths`:** same collision reports `collision.mode` under `in`,
   but should report top-level `collision` removal under own-key checks.
3. **`resolvePersistCandidateForWrite` / `writeConfigFile`:** a `nextConfig` that
   inherits a peer key (for example `commands`) can persist the prototype payload
   into `openclaw.json` instead of dropping the non-own key.

## Why This Change Was Made

`Object.hasOwn(obj, key)` is the correct primitive for own-key membership and
matches the helpers' existing `Object.keys` / `Object.entries` traversal. Five
`in` checks become `Object.hasOwn` with no new config/env surface.

## User Impact

**Before:** Callers that hand write-prepare a non-plain object (custom prototype
or inherited peer key) can persist prototype payloads or keep stale own keys that
exist only via inheritance on the peer.

**After:** Only own keys participate in merge patches, changed-path sets, and
runtime-shape projection. Inherited peer keys are treated as absent.

## Evidence

- `src/config/io.write-prepare.ts` — five `key in …` → `Object.hasOwn(…)` sites
- Discriminating regressions in `src/config/io.write-prepare.test.ts`
  - merge: own on base / inherited on target → `{ collision: null }`
  - changed paths: same fixture → `["collision", "safe.mode"]`
  - `resolvePersistCandidateForWrite` caller path drops inherited peer key
- Production persistence regression in `src/config/io.write-config.test.ts`
  - real `writeConfigFile` against a temp `openclaw.json`

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** Config persistence no longer adopts
  prototype-only peer keys from `nextConfig` during write preparation.
- **Canonical reachability path:**

```text
writeConfigFile(nextConfig)
  → resolvePersistCandidateForWrite
  → createMergePatch(runtimeConfig, nextConfig)
  → Object.hasOwn membership (not `in`)
  → applyMergePatch → validate → write openclaw.json
```

- **Boundary crossed:** local-runtime; production `createConfigIO().writeConfigFile`
  against a real temp `~/.openclaw/openclaw.json` (HOME isolated). No mocks of
  write-prepare helpers. `nextConfig` inherits `commands` and only owns `gateway`.
- **Shared helper / provider constraint check:** N/A (local config IO). Own-key
  semantics align with existing `Object.keys` traversal in the same helpers.
- **Real environment tested:** macOS Darwin 24.3.0 arm64, Node v22.22.0, branch
  `codex/fix-io-write-prepare-hasown` rebased onto `upstream/main`.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/config/io.write-prepare.test.ts --reporter=verbose
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/config/io.write-config.test.ts \
    -t 'drops keys that exist only on the next-config prototype' --reporter=verbose
```

- **Evidence after fix:**

```text
 ✓ config io write prepare > ignores prototype-chain keys when building merge patches
 ✓ config io write prepare > preserves authored keys whose names match Object.prototype members
 ✓ config io write prepare > persists caller changes without adopting inherited peer keys
 ✓ config io write prepare > ignores prototype-chain keys when collecting changed paths
 …
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  52 passed (52)

 ✓ config io write > writeConfigFile drops keys that exist only on the next-config prototype 228ms
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  1 passed | 71 skipped (72)
```

Persisted file after fix (redacted temp HOME):

```text
gateway.port = 19001
Object.hasOwn(persisted, "commands") = false
# meta.lastTouched* stamped by write path; commands not resurrected from prototype
```

Before-fix probe (same fixtures / write path with `in` restored temporarily):

```text
 × ignores prototype-chain keys when building merge patches
   Expected: { safe: { mode: "cloud" }, collision: null }
   Received: { safe: { mode: "cloud" }, collision: { mode: "inherited-target" } }
 × persists caller changes without adopting inherited peer keys

   Received: ["collision.mode", "safe.mode"]

writeConfigFile before-fix: Object.hasOwn(persisted, "commands") === true
  persisted.commands === { ownerDisplay: "raw" }  // leaked from nextConfig prototype
```

- **Observed result after fix:** Discriminating own/inherited collisions fail on the
  old `in` checks and pass with `Object.hasOwn`. Real `writeConfigFile` updates

target.title: fix(agents): distinguish z.ai code 1305 content rejection from generic overload
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: z.ai Coding Plan endpoint returns HTTP 429 with code 1305 deterministically when the system prompt contains "You are a personal assistant running inside OpenClaw". The current error classifier treats all 1305 responses as generic overload, showing "The AI service is temporarily overloaded" to users — which is misleading for the content-rejection case.

**Solution**: Add a `ZAI_CODE_1305_RE` pattern to detect `{"code":1305,...}` or `{"code":"1305",...}` (quoted or unquoted) in the raw error message and surface a more specific diagnostic before falling back to the generic overload message. The `classifyFailoverReason` hook in the z.ai plugin ensures code 1305 is classified as "overloaded" (provider-scoped), preventing misclassification by the generic rate-limit pattern.

**What changed**: 
- `sanitize-user-facing-text.ts`: Updated `ZAI_CODE_1305_RE` regex constant to match both `"code":1305` (unquoted number) and `"code":"1305"` (quoted string) JSON values; new check in `formatRateLimitOrOverloadedErrorCopy` that runs before `isOverloadedErrorMessage` and returns a neutral diagnostic for z.ai 1305 errors: "transient overload or a provider-side content restriction — try again later or with a different model."
- `extensions/zai/index.ts`: Added `classifyFailoverReason` hook that explicitly classifies z.ai code 1305 as "overloaded" (provider-scoped, prevents generic rate-limit classification from bypassing the diagnostic check)
- `failover-matches.test.ts`, `formatassistanterrortext.test.ts`: Updated tests to expect the new diagnostic message

**What did NOT change**:
- The `rate_limit` failover classification is preserved — backoff and fallback continue working
- Non-1305 overload errors return the original "overloaded" message unchanged
- Zhipu GLM `[1305]` format is not affected (doesn't match the JSON key pattern)

**Fixes**: #103529

## What Problem This Solves

Users onboarding a valid z.ai Coding Plan key successfully, but every chat turn fails with a misleading "overloaded" error. The real cause — the system prompt signature line triggering a provider-side content filter — is invisible. Users waste time checking quota, retrying, or switching API keys when the issue is the system prompt content.

## Root Cause

z.ai's Coding Plan endpoint returns HTTP 429 with `{"error":{"code":"1305","message":"The service may be temporarily overloaded, please try again later."}}` when the system message contains "You are a personal assistant running inside OpenClaw". This behavior is a **deterministic function of the system prompt content**, not a transient overload. Removing or altering that one line produces a 200 response.

The error classifier in `sanitize-user-facing-text.ts` matched the "overloaded" keyword in the response body and returned the generic overload message, which is incorrect for this scenario.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: Error message for z.ai code 1305 now mentions possible content restriction instead of generic overload

target.title: fix(google): stream Gemini batch JSONL output instead of res.text()
target.body:
<details>
<summary>Additional instructions</summary>

**MUST:** Keep **Allow edits from maintainers** enabled for this PR so maintainers
can help update the branch when needed.

</details>

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes a memory spike in the Gemini embedding batch download step where large batch output files are fully buffered in memory before any embedding is written to the result map.

`fetchGeminiFileContent` called `res.text()` to download the JSONL output file as a single string, then `parseGeminiBatchOutput` called `text.split("\n")` to produce a full `GeminiBatchOutputLine[]` array. Both the raw text buffer and the parsed object array exist simultaneously at peak — for a large embedding batch this roughly doubles peak heap on top of the result map.

## Why This Change Was Made

Replace the two-step buffer-then-parse approach with a streaming readline reader that consumes one JSONL line at a time and writes each embedding directly into `byCustomId`, matching the pattern already established in `extensions/voyage/embedding-batch.ts`.

Structural changes:

- **Deleted** `fetchGeminiFileContent` — returned the full JSONL body as a `string`.
- **Deleted** `parseGeminiBatchOutput` — split the string and mapped it to `GeminiBatchOutputLine[]`.
- **Added** `readGeminiBatchOutputContent` — wraps `Response.body` with `Readable.fromWeb` + `readline.Interface`, applies each line inline, and always closes/destroys reader resources in `finally`.
- **Added** `fetchGeminiBatchOutput` — thin wrapper that builds the `:download` URL and delegates body reading to the streamed reader.

Identifier precedence (`key` / `custom_id` / `request_id`) and both error paths are preserved.

## User Impact

Peak memory for large Gemini embedding batch jobs drops from roughly `2× output file size` (raw text + parsed lines + result map) toward approximately the embedding result map size. Successful batches, partial-error batches, and empty-output error paths keep the same user-visible behavior.

## Evidence

- Pattern parity with `extensions/voyage/embedding-batch.ts` streamed JSONL reader
- Focused regression: delayed mid-line chunked `ReadableStream` body through production `runGeminiEmbeddingBatches`
- Real `node:http` Transfer-Encoding chunked download against production caller with peak-heap before/after

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** Gemini embedding batch download no longer holds the full JSONL text and a full parsed-line array in memory at the same time while populating `byCustomId`.
- **Canonical reachability path:** `runGeminiEmbeddingBatches` → `fetchGeminiBatchOutput` → `withRemoteHttpResponse` → `readGeminiBatchOutputContent` (`Readable.fromWeb` + `readline`) → per-line `byCustomId.set`.
- **Boundary crossed:** local-runtime; real Node `http.createServer` on `127.0.0.1` serving a ~22 MiB JSONL body with 22,823 on-wire chunks (no `Content-Length`), fetched through production SSRF-guarded `withRemoteHttpResponse` with `allowPrivateNetwork`.
- **Shared helper / provider constraint check:** Mirrors Voyage's provider-local streamed JSONL reader; no new config/env. Google Batch API output remains JSONL with per-line `key`/`response`/`error`.
- **Real environment tested:** macOS (darwin 24.3.0), Node 22 (`--expose-gc --import tsx`), branch `fix/gemini-batch-streaming-jsonl-reader`.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**

```text
$ node --expose-gc --import tsx /tmp/gemini-batch-stream-proof.mjs
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/google/embedding-batch.test.ts --reporter=verbose
```

- **Evidence after fix:**

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/google/embedding-batch.test.ts --reporter=verbose
```

target.title: fix(config): reject unsupported MCP disabled config
target.body:
Closes #103954

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators configured an MCP server with `disabled: true` and OpenClaw silently started the server because only `enabled: false` controls MCP activation.

## Why This Change Was Made

The change migrates the unsupported inverse flag to the canonical enablement setting through `openclaw doctor --fix`, while configuration validation now reports the incorrect key with an actionable replacement. Runtime behavior continues to read only the canonical setting.

## User Impact

Operators receive a clear configuration error instead of unexpectedly spawning an MCP server. Existing boolean `disabled` entries can be repaired automatically with `openclaw doctor --fix`.

## Evidence

### Real isolated CLI proof

Executed from PR head `f53982039f67` with Node `v24.14.0`, using isolated `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH` and `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` values and no real credentials. The configured stdio command was `/usr/bin/touch $MARKER`, so any process start would leave an observable marker.

Before repair, `openclaw config validate --json` exited 1 and reported:

```json
{
  "valid": false,
  "issues": [
    {
      "path": "mcp.servers.proof-disabled.disabled",
      "message": "unsupported key \"disabled\"; use \"enabled: false\" instead, then run \"openclaw doctor --fix\" to migrate existing config"
    }
  ]
}
```

`openclaw doctor --fix --non-interactive` exited 0 and printed:

```text
Legacy config keys detected
- mcp.servers uses the unsupported "disabled" key; use "enabled: false" instead.

Doctor changes
Moved mcp.servers.proof-disabled.disabled true → enabled false.

Updated config: $CONFIG
Doctor complete.
```

The rewritten entry contained the canonical field and no `disabled` key:

```json
{
  "enabled": false,
  "command": "/usr/bin/touch",
  "args": ["$MARKER"],
  "transport": "stdio"
}
```

After repair, `openclaw config validate --json` exited 0 with `{"valid":true,"warnings":[]}`.

For the post-repair process-start check, the marker was removed and the actual MCP runtime probe was run:

```console
$ openclaw mcp probe --json
{
  "servers": {},
  "tools": [],
  "diagnostics": []
}
$ test -e "$MARKER" && echo present || echo absent
absent
```

A named probe also rejected the server before launch: `MCP server "proof-disabled" is disabled ... Run openclaw mcp configure proof-disabled --enable before probing it.`

### Contract and automated validation

- OpenClaw filters `mcp.servers` entries with `enabled: false` before session MCP runtime materialization (`src/agents/bundle-mcp-config.ts`).
- Direct upstream Codex source inspection at [`5c19155cbd93`](https://github.com/openai/codex/commit/5c19155cbd93bfa099016e7487259f61669823ff) confirmed that `enabled` defaults to true, `false` means skip initialization, and the connection manager filters disabled servers before spawning them (`codex-rs/config/src/mcp_types.rs`, `codex-rs/codex-mcp/src/connection_manager.rs`).
- Focused config and doctor tests passed: 237 assertions across the relevant test shards.
- Core TypeScript check passed with `pnpm tsgo:core`.
- Regression coverage verifies both inverse-value migration and preservation of an explicitly configured `enabled` value.

## AI-assisted contribution

Implemented with Codex; targeted tests, core typechecking, direct upstream contract inspection, and isolated real CLI proof were completed before submission.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Telegram `@username` target resolution could wait indefinitely when the Bot API `getChat` request stalled before headers or while reading the response body.

## Why This Change Was Made

Raw Telegram `getChat` lookups now use the existing Telegram `getchat` timeout budget and compose it with any caller abort signal through the shared plugin SDK timeout helper. Runtime target resolution and doctor repair pass the account timeout setting, while the timer remains active until the response body read finishes.

## User Impact

Telegram setup, doctor repair, and direct-message target resolution can now recover from stalled Bot API lookups instead of leaving users waiting without feedback.

## Evidence

Exact head after shared-helper refactor: `a7613eaaf24d18a457899d8ea852096b7e864808`.

Implementation update after ClawSweeper review:

- Replaced the local Telegram `AbortController`/timer composer with `buildTimeoutAbortSignal` from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/extension-shared`.
- Kept cleanup in the existing outer `finally`, so the shared deadline remains active through `readResponseWithLimit()` and covers both pre-header and mid-body stalls.
- Updated the focused timeout test to assert the shared helper's `TimeoutError: request timed out` abort reason.

```text
git diff --check -- extensions/telegram/src/api-fetch.ts extensions/telegram/src/api-fetch.test.ts
```

```text
node --import tsx --input-type=module
```

Harness shape: local HTTP Bot API endpoint, production `lookupTelegramChatId()` path, normal fetch transport, `apiRoot` pointed at the local endpoint, redacted bot token, no mocked adapter. The endpoint deliberately stalls before headers for one request and stalls during the JSON response body for the second request.

Redacted transcript:

```text
proof: controlled local stalled Bot API through Telegram getChat target-resolution helper
apiRoot: http://127.0.0.1:<redacted-port>
timeout-config: timeoutSeconds=1 supplied, getchat method budget floors to existing 15000ms minimum
server: accepted /bot<redacted-token>/getChat?chat_id=%40header-stall
[fetch-timeout] fetch timeout after 15000ms (elapsed 15001ms) operation=telegram-getchat-lookup url=http://127.0.0.1:<redacted-port>/bot<redacted-token>/getChat
target-resolution: header-stall result=null elapsed=15127ms

server: request closed /bot<redacted-token>/getChat?chat_id=%40header-stall after 15104ms
server: accepted /bot<redacted-token>/getChat?chat_id=%40body-stall
[fetch-timeout] fetch timeout after 15000ms (elapsed 15001ms) operation=telegram-getchat-lookup url=http://127.0.0.1:<redacted-port>/bot<redacted-token>/getChat
target-resolution: body-stall result=null elapsed=15022ms
server: response closed /bot<redacted-token>/getChat?chat_id=%40body-stall after 15013ms
server: request closed /bot<redacted-token>/getChat?chat_id=%40body-stall after 15013ms
observed-requests: /bot<redacted-token>/getChat?chat_id=%40header-stall, /bot<redacted-token>/getChat?chat_id=%40body-stall
```

- A stalled pre-header `getChat` request returns `null` through the Telegram target-resolution helper after the existing 15s `getchat` budget.
- A stalled mid-body `getChat` response also returns `null` after the same budget, proving the timeout remains active through response-body reads.
- The local Bot API server observes client-side connection closure after each timeout.
- The shared SDK helper emits the existing `[fetch-timeout]` diagnostic with operation `telegram-getchat-lookup`.
- `timeoutSeconds=1` was intentionally supplied to prove the existing method budget remains the floor; `getchat` still uses the canonical 15000ms minimum.

Known limits:

- This is controlled-network runtime proof, not a live Telegram Bot API outage reproduction.
- Remote Testbox/Crabbox proof was unavailable in this environment because no working `crabbox` binary was present; this used the documented narrow local fallback plus GitHub CI.

target.title: fix(github-copilot): bound Copilot token exchange fetch timeout
target.body:
<details>
<summary>Additional instructions</summary>

**MUST:** Keep **Allow edits from maintainers** enabled for this PR so maintainers
can help update the branch when needed.

</details>

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where GitHub Copilot API token exchange could hang forever after a cache miss when `api.<domain>/copilot_internal/v2/token` stopped responding.

`resolveCopilotApiToken()` in `src/plugin-sdk/provider-auth.ts` issued a bare `fetch` with no `AbortSignal` / timeout. Callers across model auth, embeddings, media understanding, and simple-completion refresh all reuse this helper, so a stalled exchange left those surfaces waiting indefinitely.

Sibling paths already had deadlines:

- GitHub Copilot device-code / token-poll OAuth uses `AbortSignal.timeout(30_000)`
- Copilot embedding `/models` discovery timeout is covered by open PR #102886

This PR covers the remaining exchange path itself.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add a fixed internal 30-second per-request deadline via `AbortSignal.timeout` on the Copilot token-exchange fetch, aligned with `COPILOT_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS` in the Copilot OAuth helper. Map `AbortError` / `TimeoutError` to:

`Copilot token exchange timed out after 30000ms`

Preserve the original abort cause with `{ cause: error }`. The published `resolveCopilotApiToken` signature is unchanged — no public `timeoutMs` override.

## User Impact

**Before:** After Copilot token cache miss/expiry, a hung GitHub token-exchange endpoint could block Copilot model/embedding/auth refresh forever.

**After:** The exchange aborts at 30s with an explicit timeout error instead of hanging.

## Evidence

- `src/plugin-sdk/provider-auth.ts` — fixed internal `AbortSignal.timeout(30_000)` on `resolveCopilotApiToken` exchange fetch; timeout errors preserve `{ cause }`
- Regression: `src/plugin-sdk/provider-auth.test.ts`
  - success path asserts the exchange request carries an `AbortSignal`
  - hung mocked fetch aborts with the 30s timeout message
  - real `node:http` loopback that accepts TCP but never writes headers aborts via transport `fetchImpl` race (~250ms) while production still installs the 30s signal

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** Copilot token exchange no longer leaves the GitHub `copilot_internal/v2/token` HTTP request unbounded when the remote endpoint stops responding before headers return.
- **Canonical reachability path:**

```text
cache miss / expired github-copilot.token.json
  → resolveCopilotApiToken (plugin-sdk/provider-auth)
  → GET api.<domain>/copilot_internal/v2/token
  → AbortSignal.timeout(30_000)
  → TimeoutError → "Copilot token exchange timed out after 30000ms"
```

Callers that hit this helper include `extensions/github-copilot` token/models/embeddings paths, `src/agents/simple-completion-runtime.ts`, and `src/media-understanding/image.ts`.

- **Boundary crossed:** local-runtime; production `resolveCopilotApiToken` exercised against a real Node HTTP server that accepts the connection and never sends response bytes (no live GitHub credential / blackhole required).
- **Shared helper / provider constraint check:** Timeout value matches sibling Copilot OAuth request timeout (`30_000`). Published Plugin SDK signature unchanged (no `timeoutMs` param). Does not change device-code login or embedding `/models` discovery (the latter is #102886).
- **Real environment tested:** macOS (Darwin), Node v22.22.0, branch `fix/copilot-token-exchange-timeout`.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/plugin-sdk/provider-auth.test.ts -t "aborts hung Copilot token exchange|plus-signed Copilot token" --reporter=verbose
```

- **Evidence after fix:**

```text
 ✓ accepts plus-signed Copilot token expiry strings 860ms
 ✓ aborts hung Copilot token exchange instead of waiting forever 1018ms
 ✓ aborts hung Copilot token exchange over HTTP transport 797ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  3 passed | 19 skipped (22)
 Duration  23.07s
```

- **Observed result after fix:**
  - Happy-path exchange request includes an `AbortSignal`
  - Mock hung fetch rejects with `Copilot token exchange timed out after 30000ms`
  - Real loopback hang (TCP accept, no headers) rejects with `Copilot token exchange timed out after 30000ms` in ~797ms wall time, proving undici/`fetch` honors abort on a live socket while the published helper keeps the fixed 30s deadline
- **What was not tested:** Live `api.github.com/copilot_internal/v2/token` blackhole with a real GitHub OAuth token; post-header body stalls after headers return.
- **Fix classification:** Root cause fix.

- [x] Change is focused and does not mix unrelated concerns
- Single commit on `upstream/main`; no bundled `scripts/` or release-script changes

target.title: fix(outbound): preserve backticks on <code> tags with attributes
target.body: Closes #104117 ## What Problem This Solves Fixes an issue where inline code blocks emitted by models with attributes—such as `foo()`—lost their backtick wrapping when OpenClaw converted outbound HTML to plain text for channels. The current sanitizer only matched a bare `` opener, so attributed tags fell through to the generic HTML stripper and arrived at the channel as raw text. ## Why This Change Was Made Updated the regex in `src/infra/outbound/sanitize-text.ts` to accept optional attributes on the opening `` tag (`/]*)?>(.*?)<\/code>/gi`), matching the existing treatment of `]*>` and `]*>` in the same function. Added a focused unit test covering `class` and multiple attributes. ## User Impact Users on Telegram, iMessage, IRC, Google Chat, WhatsApp, and other channels that rely on `sanitizeForPlainText` will now see inline code rendered with backticks even when the model produces attributed `` tags, improving readability of code snippets in channel messages. ## Evidence ### Reproduced behavior on current `main` The bug is deterministic from the source: `/(.*?)<\/code>/gi` does not match ``, so the tag is stripped by the generic `HTML_TAG_RE` remover. ### After-fix runtime proof (public SDK export) The patched helper is the same `openclaw/plugin-sdk/channel-outbound` export that Telegram, iMessage, and other channel adapters import at runtime: ```bash $ ./node_modules/.bin/tsx -e "import { sanitizeForPlainText } from 'openclaw/plugin-sdk/channel-outbound'; console.log('attributed:', sanitizeForPlainText('foo()')); console.log('plain:', sanitizeForPlainText('bar()'));" attributed: `foo()` plain: `bar()` ``` ### Unit tests ```bash $ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/infra/outbound/sanitize-text.test.ts ✓ |unit-fast| src/infra/outbound/sanitize-text.test.ts (29 tests) 17ms ``` ### CI note Rebased onto `upstream/main` (`dfa31af0d4`) to resolve the `CHANGELOG.md does not contain a release section for 2026.7.2` failure in the QA Smoke CI build. That error was caused by the branch being behind `main` (still on `2026.6.11`) while the smoke packaging step expected the current release-train version; it is unrelated to this code change.

**Behavior or issue addressed**: Agent-facing descriptors and public docs said `memory/*.md` even though the runtime already walks `memory/` recursively and indexes nested files such as `memory/YYYY-MM/YYYY-MM-DD.md`. target.title: fix(cli): one-shot agent --local runs never export OTel diagnostics
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where one-shot `openclaw agent --local` runs would export no OTel telemetry at all when `diagnostics.otel.enabled: true` and the `diagnostics-otel` plugin are configured: zero spans, metrics, or logs reached the OTLP collector, while the same turns dispatched through the Gateway exported fine. Gateway-to-embedded fallback runs (gateway timeout or transport failure) silently dropped telemetry the same way, so exactly the runs that bypass the Gateway were invisible in tracing backends.

## Why This Change Was Made

Diagnostics exporters are plugin services and were only ever started inside the Gateway process (`startPluginServices` at gateway startup/reload); embedded CLI runs emit diagnostic events in the CLI process where nothing subscribes. The CLI now starts the `diagnostics-otel` service around embedded agent runs via a scoped, non-activating plugin load that honors the same plugin-enablement config as the Gateway, and flushes on exit: drain the async diagnostic-event queue, then shut the SDK down (force flush), bounded by a 10s timeout so an unreachable collector cannot hang the CLI. `diagnostics-prometheus` intentionally stays Gateway-only — it is a pull-based scrape server that is useless in a short-lived process and would race the Gateway for its port. No new config surface; configs without OTel enabled short-circuit before any plugin load.

## User Impact

Operators running one-shot `openclaw agent --local` turns (and runs that fall back from the Gateway to the embedded agent) now get the same OTel traces, metrics, and logs as Gateway-executed turns, flushed before the process exits. Setups without OTel export enabled are unaffected.

## Evidence

- Live before/after on macOS against a local Arize Phoenix OTLP collector: before, one-shot `--local` runs produced zero spans while Gateway runs exported fine; after, a one-shot run logs `diagnostics-otel: logs exporter enabled (OTLP/Protobuf)` and `openclaw.harness.run`, `openclaw.run`, and `openclaw.model.call` spans (with `gen_ai.*` attributes) arrive in Phoenix seconds after the process exits.
- New focused tests: `src/plugins/one-shot-diagnostics.test.ts` covers config gating (no plugin load when OTel is off), the scoped non-activating load, exporter allowlist filtering, drain-before-stop ordering, and the flush timeout bound; `src/commands/agent-via-gateway.test.ts` adds cases for start/flush ordering around local runs, flush when the embedded run fails, run survival when exporter startup fails, exporter start on gateway-to-embedded fallback, and no exporter on Gateway dispatch. Both files pass (9 + 73 tests) rebased on current `main`.
- `pnpm build` clean with no `[INEFFECTIVE_DYNAMIC_IMPORT]` warnings; `tsgo` core and test lanes clean; oxfmt/oxlint clean on touched files. Validation ran locally via `scripts/run-vitest.mjs` (remote Testbox was unavailable in this environment).

target.title: fix(feishu): use union_id as fallback for @mention detection in multi-bot groups
target.body:
## Problem

Fixes #40768

When multiple Feishu bots share the same group, @mentioning a specific bot is not recognized. The bot logs `message in group ... did not mention bot` even though it's correctly mentioned.

## Root Cause

Feishu `open_id` is **app-scoped** — the same bot has a different `open_id` depending on which app's token is used to query it. Confirmed by querying the same message with two different bot tokens:

```
# Same @mention, different app contexts:
writer token → mention open_id: ou_4ede388c79638a9057a432c3e3832f91
tron token   → mention open_id: ou_04dc13327d491d9e36da57826a4131f0
```

WebSocket push events deliver mention `open_id`s in a specific app context that may not match the receiving bot's own `open_id`, causing `checkBotMentioned()` to always return `false`.

## Fix

`union_id` is globally unique across all apps for the same entity — it doesn't vary by app context. This PR:

1. Fetches `union_id` alongside `open_id` from `bot/v3/info` at startup
2. Stores it in a new `botUnionIds` map in monitor state
3. Passes it through to `checkBotMentioned()` as a fallback
4. Matches mentions by `union_id` when `open_id` doesn't match

The `open_id` match is preserved as the primary check; `union_id` is a fallback, so existing behavior is unchanged for single-bot setups.

## Files Changed

- `types.ts`: add `botUnionId` to `FeishuProbeResult`
- `probe.ts`: extract `union_id` from `bot/v3/info` response
- `monitor.startup.ts`: propagate `botUnionId` through `FeishuMonitorBotIdentity`
- `monitor.state.ts`: add `botUnionIds` map with proper clear/delete
- `monitor.account.ts`: store/clear `botUnionId`, pass to `handleFeishuMessage`
- `bot.ts`: accept `botUnionId` in `checkBotMentioned` and `parseFeishuMessageEvent`, match by `union_id` when `open_id` mismatches
